items.headline: Google Launches AI Tool to Add Interactivity to E-books
items.excerpt: Expert Intelligence lets readers query e-books bought from the Google Play store, along with other features, and includes more than 100,000 titles, mostly trade nonfiction, from such publishers as Penguin Random House, Macmillan, and Bloomsbury.

items.headline: AI Use in The Scholarly Kitchen
items.excerpt: Some thoughts on the reader response the Scholarly Kitchen has seen regarding AI use by authors, a recent Nature News article on the efficacy of AI detection tools, and why it's important to keep experimenting to figure out what's ethically acceptable.

items.headline: Excluded lawyers in Anthropic case want their fees
items.excerpt: Appeals have been filed by firms that were never appointed as class counsel but who nonetheless worked the case on behalf of authors and publishers.

items.headline: How Claude watermarking works: Some accuse Anthropic of compliance theatre
items.excerpt: Commentators find it problematic that the watermark gets applied when Claude is used for assistive tasks rather than generative tasks.

items.headline: Amazon is buying and scanning books to train AI
items.excerpt: But breathless coverage misses the fact that most of these books may be out of date, undesirable to readers, and not valuable per se.

items.headline: Publishing is unfairly excluding disabled authors using AI
items.excerpt: Blanket bans on AI use are unfairly excluding disabled authors using the technology responsibly, argues David James.

items.headline: The AI ‘Ghosts’ Contaminating Academic Publishing
items.excerpt: “The academic record is being quietly haunted” by researchers with names like Elena Vasquez and Marcus Chen.

items.headline: Inside the Warehouse Where Amazon Scans and Destroys Books for AI Training

items.headline: Anthropic’s Text Watermarking Proves AI Companies Do Not Care at All About Writing
items.excerpt: AI companies see words as interchangeable and have zero clue how to judge the “quality” of writing.

items.headline: News Summary: Are Amazon and Other AI Companies Destroying Books to Train AI?

items.headline: These are all of the new Spotify Audibook features

items.headline: AI Companies are buying hardcover books and destroying them
items.excerpt: The biggest fear for people who want to see books preserved through the training process is that AI firms will callously pulp rare books that can never be replaced.
